title: The Cairo Lab That Chose an Accreditation Egypt Did Not Require
dek: In 2007 Hend El Sherbini decided her mother's laboratory chain would seek CAP accreditation, though no Egyptian rule asked for it and doctors said it could not be done.

story.founder: Hend El Sherbini and Moamena Kamel
story.event: Deciding in 2007 to pursue College of American Pathologists accreditation for a Cairo laboratory
story.summary: In 2007 Hend El Sherbini, managing director of the Egyptian laboratory chain Al Mokhtabar, which grew from a single laboratory her mother Dr Moamena Kamel opened in Cairo in 1979, decided to seek accreditation from the College of American Pathologists although Egypt did not require it. The founding laboratory was accredited in 2010; the accreditation lapsed in April 2014 when unrest delayed CAP's inspection, and the group's new central laboratory in Cairo was accredited in 2018.
paragraphs: In 2007 Hend El Sherbini was running Al Mokhtabar, a chain of medical laboratories in Egypt that had grown from a single laboratory her mother, Dr Moamena Kamel, opened in Cairo in 1979. That year, by her own account, the laboratory was doing referral testing for the American Embassy in Cairo, and through that work she was introduced to the College of American Pathologists and its accreditation programme.

Nothing obliged her to go further. Accreditation, she later said, was not required in Egypt. Her mother, a Cairo University professor of immunology whom she describes as a pathologist, had obtained ISO 9001 for her laboratory in 1998 but wanted a standard written for clinical laboratories, which ISO did not then offer. El Sherbini had trained at Cairo University's medical faculty and worked as a researcher at the US Centers for Disease Control. When she came home to the family laboratory, in 2001 by one of her accounts, most samples were sent abroad, she said, because people did not trust Egyptian tests.

She decided that year to pursue CAP accreditation. "We ordered the CAP checklists and got to work," she recalled. Doctors told her, "You cannot do that." At first, she admitted, nobody knew what the requirements were. Help came from CAP counterparts in the United States and Europe, and she said that working through it together gave the staff a sense of ownership.

The laboratory accredited in 2010 was, according to the group's 2015 listing prospectus, MK Lab, the one her mother had founded, and the only private laboratory in Egypt to have received CAP accreditation. In 2012 Al Mokhtabar was acquired by Integrated Diagnostics Holdings, the group built around Al Borg, a rival founded in 1990 by four doctors, and El Sherbini became its chief executive. The accreditation then lapsed. It expired in April 2014, the prospectus said, because unrest in Egypt delayed CAP sending an inspector. In 2018 the group's new central laboratory in Cairo earned it again. El Sherbini later said Al Mokhtabar's performance indicators are built on the CAP checklists, which has helped each time it opens a new location.

quote.text: The dynamic nature of their philosophy laid more stress upon the process through which perfection was sought than upon perfection itself.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: Okakura is describing how Taoist and Zen artists thought about perfection, not laboratories. Yet this story bears him out: the accreditation is renewed every two years, lapsed once when no inspector could come, and was earned again in a new building. What lasted was the practice of working to the checklist.

reflection: You know from the bench why El Sherbini's doctors doubted her. An accreditation nobody requires is easy to postpone, because the work it asks for stays invisible until something goes wrong. What she did first was small: she ordered the checklists and let them show the gap.

talQen is built for laboratories on that road, and it is tempting to picture the day a lab passes its inspection. Okakura points elsewhere. In this story the certificate lapsed when no inspector could travel, and the habits stayed. The labs you serve will need help with the ordinary weeks between inspections more than with the inspection itself.
invitation: Choose one clause of a standard you work to, ISO 15189 or another, and read it this morning as an inspector would. Note one place where your own work would not yet meet it, and leave the fixing for another day.

cross_checks.claim: Dr Moamena Kamel founded her first laboratory, a single site in Cairo, in 1979
The laboratory first earned CAP accreditation in 2010
El Sherbini ran Al Mokhtabar from 2004 and became chief executive of Integrated Diagnostics Holdings in 2012
Al Borg was founded in 1990 by four doctors, IDH was formed around it in 2008, and IDH acquired Al Mokhtabar in 2012
The CAP accreditation expired in April 2014 and the new Cairo central laboratory was certified in 2018

research_notes: The slate entry was wrong on the company: Dr Moamena Kamel did not found Al Borg. IDH's history page and its 2015 prospectus both say Al Borg was founded in 1990 by a group of four doctors, and that Dr Kamel founded her first laboratory, MK Lab, in 1979; MK Lab merged with Al Mokhtabar in 2004, and in 2012 IDH (created in 2008 when Abraaj bought 76.8 per cent of Al Borg) acquired Al Mokhtabar. The story is therefore told through Al Mokhtabar. No interview with Dr Kamel herself could be found in English or Arabic, and the 1979 founding is documented only in a line or two, so the episode is her daughter's documented 2007 decision to seek CAP accreditation, told mainly in El Sherbini's own words (CAP, 2021). Disagreements: (1) Kamel's field: IDH, its prospectus, IFC and Lionesses of Africa call her a professor of immunology; El Sherbini, in the CAP interview, calls her a pathologist. The story gives both, attributed. (2) Who founded what: CAP says Kamel founded Al Mokhtabar in 1979; IDH says she founded MK Lab, which later merged with Al Mokhtabar. The story says she opened a single laboratory in 1979 from which the chain grew. (3) When El Sherbini joined: 2001 in the Lionesses of Africa answers; 2004 in the CAP article and as managing director from 2004 in the prospectus. The story says she came home in 2001 'by one of her accounts' and was running Al Mokhtabar by 2007. (4) Continuity of accreditation: in 2021 El Sherbini said Al Mokhtabar had held CAP accreditation for 'ten straight years', but the 2015 prospectus says it expired in April 2014 because turmoil delayed CAP's inspection, and IDH's 2018 announcement records the new Mega Lab's certification after the two older A-labs, 'one of which was CAP certified', were replaced. The story follows the contemporary filings and does not repeat the ten-year claim. (5) ISO 9001 in 1998: El Sherbini attributes it to her mother's laboratory; the prospectus accreditation table lists an ISO 9001 (TUV) certification from 1998 whose row is ambiguous in the PDF layout, so the story attributes the date to El Sherbini. ISO 9001 is strictly a certification, so the story avoids calling it accreditation. (6) Firsts: CAP and IDH describe the laboratory as the only CAP-accredited private laboratory in Egypt at various dates; the story limits this to the prospectus's 2015 statement. (7) El Sherbini's PhD: IFC and Lionesses say Cairo University, CAP says the United States; the story mentions neither. Outcome numbers (branch counts from 218 to more than 500, test volumes of 27 to 30 million) vary by entity and year, so the story uses none. Funding is given as bootstrapped because Al Mokhtabar was a family-owned business until its 2012 sale to IDH; a 2007 memorandum to sell 49 per cent to Al Muhaidib & Sons was never completed (prospectus, legal proceedings). The prospectus PDF loads but the checker may not read its text. Ownership today: El Sherbini and Kamel jointly own Hena Holdings, IDH's largest shareholder; this is not needed in the story. The Okakura line comes from his discussion of Taoist and Zen ideas of perfection in art and is applied here by analogy.
